text:
It is necessary to design a link-layer protocol between two hosts that are directly connected over a lossless link of length [latex]3000[/latex] kilometers. Assume that the link bandwidth is [latex]10^8[/latex] bits per second and that the propagation delay in the link is [latex]5[/latex] nanoseconds per meter. Every transmitted data byte is assigned a unique sequence number.

Let [latex]N[/latex] be the minimum number of bits needed for the sequence number field in the protocol header such that:

(i) the sequence numbers do not wrap around before [latex]60[/latex] seconds, and
(ii) the maximum utilization of the link is achieved.

The value of [latex]N[/latex] is ______. (answer in integer)
solution:
Propagation delay (one-way) [latex]=3000\text{ km}\times5\text{ ns/m}=3{,}000{,}000\text{ m}\times5\text{ ns}=15{,}000{,}000\text{ ns}=15[/latex] ms, so round-trip time [latex]\text{RTT}=30[/latex] ms [latex]=0.03[/latex] s.

Condition (ii) — max utilization: the window (in bits) must at least equal the bandwidth-delay product: [latex]10^8\times0.03=3\times10^6[/latex] bits [latex]=375{,}000[/latex] bytes, requiring at least [latex]\lceil\log_2(375000)\rceil\approx19[/latex] sequence-number bits.

Condition (i) — no wraparound within 60 s: total bytes sent in [latex]60[/latex] s at full bandwidth [latex]=\dfrac{10^8\times60}{8}=750{,}000{,}000[/latex] bytes, requiring [latex]2^N\ge750{,}000{,}000[/latex], i.e. [latex]N\ge\lceil\log_2(750{,}000{,}000)\rceil=30[/latex] (since [latex]2^{29}\approx5.37\times10^8<7.5\times10^8\le2^{30}\approx1.07\times10^9[/latex]).

Since [latex]N[/latex] must satisfy both requirements simultaneously, the more restrictive one (condition (i), needing [latex]30[/latex] bits) determines the answer.

Answer: 30

text:
Consider a new TCP connection between a sender and a receiver. The receiver advertised window is constant at [latex]48[/latex] KB, the maximum segment size (MSS) is [latex]2[/latex] KB, and the slow start threshold for TCP congestion control is [latex]16[/latex] KB. Assume that there are no timeouts or duplicate acknowledgements. The number of rounds of transmission required for the congestion control algorithm of the TCP connection to reach the congestion avoidance phase is ________. (answer in integer)
Note: [latex]1 {~K}=2^{10}[/latex]
solution:
In TCP slow start, [latex]\text{cwnd}[/latex] starts at [latex]1[/latex] MSS and doubles every round-trip, until it reaches the slow-start threshold ([latex]\text{ssthresh}=16[/latex] KB), at which point congestion avoidance begins.

[latex]\begin{array}{c|c}\text{Round}&\text{cwnd}\\\hline1&2\text{ KB (1 MSS)}\\2&4\text{ KB}\\3&8\text{ KB}\\4&16\text{ KB}\end{array}[/latex]

At the end of round [latex]4[/latex], [latex]\text{cwnd}[/latex] reaches exactly [latex]16[/latex] KB, equal to [latex]\text{ssthresh}[/latex] — so it takes [latex]4[/latex] rounds of slow-start doubling before the connection is ready to switch into the congestion-avoidance phase.

Answer: 4

text: Consider the transmission of data bits [latex]110001011[/latex] over a link that uses Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) code for error detection. If the generator bit pattern is given to be [latex]1001[/latex], which one of the following options shows the remainder bit pattern appended to the data bits before transmission?
solution:
Perform binary (modulo-2) division of the data (with [latex]3[/latex] zero bits appended, since the generator [latex]1001[/latex] has degree [latex]3[/latex]) by the generator [latex]1001[/latex], where each subtraction step is simply an XOR:

Dividend: [latex]110001011000[/latex] (original data [latex]110001011[/latex] followed by [latex]000[/latex]).
Repeatedly XOR-ing the generator [latex]1001[/latex] into the leading bits wherever the current leading bit is [latex]1[/latex], and shifting along, the division terminates with remainder [latex]100[/latex].

This remainder [latex]100[/latex] is what gets appended to the original data bits to form the transmitted CRC codeword.

Answer: 100

text: Which one of the following protocols may need to broadcast some of its messages?
solution:
DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) is used by a host to automatically obtain an IP address (and other network configuration) when it first joins a network — since the host doesn't yet have an IP address (or know the server's address), its initial "DHCP Discover" message must be broadcast on the local network so that any DHCP server present can respond.

[latex]\text{SMTP}[/latex] (mail), [latex]\text{FTP}[/latex] (file transfer), and [latex]\text{HTTP}[/latex] (web) are all conventional client-server protocols that communicate with a specific, already-known server address over a normal unicast connection — they have no inherent need to broadcast.

Consider a file of size [latex]4[/latex] million bytes being transferred between two hosts connected via a path consisting of three consecutive links of bandwidth [latex]2[/latex] Mbps , [latex]500[/latex] kbps , and [latex]1[/latex] Mbps , respectively. All processing delays and propagation delays are negligible. Assume that there is no other background traffic over the path and no other additional overhead to transfer the file.

Which one of the following is the total time (in seconds) to transfer the file?
Note: [latex]1 {M}=10^{6}, 1 {k}=10^{3}[/latex]
solution:
With processing and propagation delays negligible, the effective throughput of a series of links is limited by the slowest (bottleneck) link in the path — here, [latex]500[/latex] kbps (since it's the minimum of [latex]2[/latex] Mbps, [latex]500[/latex] kbps, and [latex]1[/latex] Mbps).

File size [latex]=4\times10^6[/latex] bytes [latex]=4\times10^6\times8=32\times10^6[/latex] bits.

Total transfer time [latex]=\dfrac{32\times10^6\text{ bits}}{500\times10^3\text{ bps}}=64[/latex] seconds.

Answer: 64

text: An ISP having an address block [latex]202.16.0.0/15[/latex] assigns a block of [latex]6000[/latex] IP addresses to a client, using the classless internet domain routing (CIDR) super-netting approach. Which of the following address blocks can be assigned by the ISP?
solution:
The ISP's block [latex]202.16.0.0/15[/latex] spans two full class-B-sized blocks: all addresses from [latex]202.16.0.0[/latex] to [latex]202.17.255.255[/latex].

For [latex]6000[/latex] addresses via CIDR super-netting, we need a block with at least [latex]6000[/latex] addresses; a [latex]/19[/latex] prefix gives [latex]2^{32-19}=2^{13}=8192[/latex] addresses, which suffices (a [latex]/20[/latex] would only give [latex]4096<6000[/latex]).

A valid [latex]/19[/latex] sub-block must (a) lie entirely within [latex]202.16.0.0[/latex]-[latex]202.17.255.255[/latex], and (b) have its network address aligned to a multiple of [latex]32[/latex] in the relevant octet (since [latex]/19[/latex] leaves [latex]13[/latex] host bits, and [latex]2^{13}=8192=32\times256[/latex] addresses per block, so the 3rd octet must be a multiple of [latex]32[/latex]: [latex]0,32,64,\ldots[/latex]).

- [latex]202.16.0.0/19[/latex]: [latex]0[/latex] is a valid multiple of [latex]32[/latex], and within range. Valid.
- [latex]202.17.64.0/19[/latex]: [latex]64[/latex] is a valid multiple of [latex]32[/latex], [latex]202.17.x[/latex] is within the /15 range. Valid.
- [latex]202.16.32.0/19[/latex]: [latex]32[/latex] is a valid multiple of [latex]32[/latex]. Valid.
- [latex]202.17.24.0/19[/latex]: [latex]24[/latex] is not a multiple of [latex]32[/latex] (valid boundaries are [latex]0,32,64,\ldots[/latex]), so this is not a properly aligned [latex]/19[/latex] block. Invalid.

Answer: 202.16.0.0/19, 202.17.64.0/19, and 202.16.32.0/19 can be assigned.

text: Consider the implementation of sliding window protocol over a lossless link, with a window size of [latex]W[/latex] frames, where each frame is of size [latex]1000[/latex] bits (including header). The bandwidth of the link is [latex]100 {kbps}\left(1 {k}=10^{3}\right)[/latex] and the one-way propagation delay is [latex]100[/latex] milliseconds. Assume that processing times at the sender and receiver are zero and the transmission time of acknowledgements is also zero. Which one of the following options gives the minimum size of [latex]W[/latex] (in number of frames) required to achieve [latex]100\%[/latex] link utilization?
solution:
Transmission time [latex]T_t=\dfrac{\text{frame size}}{\text{bandwidth}}=\dfrac{1000\text{ bits}}{100\times10^3\text{ bps}}=10[/latex] ms.

For [latex]100\%[/latex] link utilization with a sliding window, the sender must be able to keep transmitting continuously until the acknowledgement of the very first frame returns, which takes [latex]T_t+2T_p[/latex] (one-way propagation to receiver, plus one-way for the ack to come back, plus zero processing/ack-transmission time).

So we need: [latex]W\cdot T_t\ge T_t+2T_p\;\Rightarrow\;W\ge1+\dfrac{2T_p}{T_t}=1+\dfrac{2\times100}{10}=1+20=21[/latex].

Answer: 21

text: Which of the following statements is/are true with respect to the interaction of a web browser with a web server using HTTP [latex]1.1[/latex]?
solution:
HTTP/1.1 introduced persistent connections and pipelining over a single TCP connection:

- True: Multiple objects of the same webpage, if hosted on the same server, can be fetched over one persistent TCP connection — this is exactly the point of persistent connections.
- False: A single TCP connection is between one client and one specific server; objects stored on a different server require a separate TCP connection to that server. So this statement is false.
- True: HTTP/1.1 supports pipelining — a client can send a new request before the response to a previous request has been fully received, over the same connection.
- True: Since the TCP connection persists (is not closed after one request/response), multiple different webpages/resources from the same server can be downloaded over that same single connection, one after another.

Answer: Statements 1, 3, and 4 are true (same-server multi-object download, pipelining, multiple pages over one connection); statement about different servers over the same connection is false.

text: With respect to a TCP connection between a client and a server, which one of the following statements is true?
solution:
Checking each statement about a TCP connection:

- TCP uses a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), not a two-way handshake — false.
- Either side (client or server) is free to initiate connection termination first; the server is not required to wait for the client — false.
- TCP is a full-duplex protocol — data can flow in both directions simultaneously — so "half-duplex" is false.
- TCP supports simultaneous close: both client and server can send a FIN at (roughly) the same time, and each independently acknowledges the other's FIN. This is a valid connection-termination scenario in TCP's state machine.

Answer: The client and server can initiate closing of the connection at the same time

Suppose we are transmitting frames between two nodes using the Stop-and-Wait protocol. The frame size is 3000 bits. The transmission rate of the channel is 2000 bps (bits/second) and the propagation delay between the two nodes is 100 milliseconds. Assume that the processing times at the source and destination are negligible. Also, assume that the size of the acknowledgment packet is negligible.  
Which ONE of the following most accurately gives the channel utilization for the above scenario in percentage?

Transmission time [latex]T_t=\dfrac{3000\text{ bits}}{2000\text{ bps}}=1.5[/latex] s. Propagation delay [latex]T_p=0.1[/latex] s (one-way).

Utilization [latex]=\dfrac{T_t}{T_t+2T_p}=\dfrac{1.5}{1.5+0.2}=\dfrac{1.5}{1.7}\approx0.8823=88.23\%[/latex]

Answer: 88.23

Consider a network that uses Ethernet and IPv4. Assume that IPv4 headers do not use any options field. Each Ethernet frame can carry a maximum of 1500 bytes in its data field. A UDP segment is transmitted. The payload (data) in the UDP segment is 7488 bytes.
Which ONE of the following choices has the CORRECT total number of fragments transmitted and the size of the last fragment including IPv4 header?
solution:
Ethernet frame data field max [latex]=1500[/latex] bytes; IPv4 header [latex]=20[/latex] bytes (no options), so max IP data per fragment [latex]=1500-20=1480[/latex] bytes — conveniently already a multiple of [latex]8[/latex], so no further rounding needed.

The UDP segment (header [latex]8[/latex] bytes [latex]+[/latex] payload [latex]7488[/latex] bytes [latex]=7496[/latex] bytes) becomes the IP datagram's data, which must be fragmented:
[latex]7496\div1480=5.06\ldots[/latex], so [latex]5[/latex] full fragments of [latex]1480[/latex] bytes ([latex]7400[/latex] bytes) plus a final fragment of [latex]7496-7400=96[/latex] bytes of data.

Total fragments [latex]=5+1=6[/latex]. Last fragment's total size (including its own [latex]20[/latex]-byte IP header) [latex]=96+20=116[/latex] bytes.

Answer: 6 fragments, 116 bytes

text:
A machine receives an IPv4 datagram. The protocol field of the IPv4 header has the protocol number of a protocol X.
Which ONE of the following is NOT a possible candidate for X?
solution:
The IPv4 protocol field identifies which higher-layer protocol's data the datagram carries, using standard registered numbers: ICMP [latex]=1[/latex], IGMP [latex]=2[/latex], OSPF [latex]=89[/latex] — all of these run directly over IP and have their own dedicated protocol number.

RIP, however, is not carried directly over IP; it runs as an application-layer protocol on top of UDP (using UDP port [latex]520[/latex]). So an IP datagram carrying RIP traffic would have its protocol field set to UDP's number ([latex]17[/latex]), never a dedicated "RIP" protocol number.

Answer: Routing Information Protocol (RIP)

text:
Consider the following statements:

(i) Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) provides a mapping from an IP address to the corresponding hardware (link-layer) address.
(ii) A single TCP segment from a sender S to a receiver R cannot carry both data from S to R and acknowledgement for a segment from R to S.

Which ONE of the following is CORRECT?
solution:
(i) ARP maps IP addresses to hardware (MAC) addresses: this is exactly ARP's definition — TRUE.

(ii) "A single TCP segment cannot carry both data and an acknowledgement": this is FALSE. TCP is full-duplex, and a very common optimization called piggybacking lets a single outgoing segment simultaneously carry new data (from S to R) and an acknowledgement field (ACKing previously received data from R) — the TCP header always has an ACK field available regardless of whether the segment also carries data.

Answer: (i) is TRUE and (ii) is FALSE

text: Suppose a message of size 15000 bytes is transmitted from a source to a destination using IPv4 protocol via two routers as shown in the figure. Each router has a defined maximum transmission unit (MTU) as shown in the figure, including IP header. The number of fragments that will be delivered to the destination is _________. (Answer in integer)
solution:
Assume the standard [latex]20[/latex]-byte IPv4 header (no options), so the original datagram is [latex]15000+20=15020[/latex] bytes.

At Router-1 (MTU [latex]5000[/latex]): max data per fragment [latex]=5000-20=4980[/latex] bytes, but fragment data must be a multiple of [latex]8[/latex] bytes, so usable data per (non-last) fragment [latex]=\lfloor4980/8\rfloor\times8=4976[/latex] bytes.
[latex]15000[/latex] bytes of data [latex]\div4976\approx3.01[/latex]: so [latex]3[/latex] full fragments of [latex]4976[/latex] bytes ([latex]14928[/latex] bytes) plus a final fragment of [latex]15000-14928=72[/latex] bytes. Total after Router-1: 4 fragments.

At Router-2 (MTU [latex]3000[/latex]): each fragment bigger than [latex]3000[/latex] bytes must be split again; the small [latex]72[/latex]-byte-data fragment (total size [latex]92[/latex] bytes) passes straight through unchanged.
Max data per new sub-fragment [latex]=3000-20=2980[/latex], rounded down to a multiple of [latex]8[/latex]: [latex]\lfloor2980/8\rfloor\times8=2976[/latex] bytes.
Each of the [latex]3[/latex] big fragments (data [latex]=4976[/latex] bytes) splits into: one sub-fragment of [latex]2976[/latex] bytes, plus a final sub-fragment of [latex]4976-2976=2000[/latex] bytes — [latex]2[/latex] sub-fragments each, so [latex]3\times2=6[/latex] sub-fragments total.

Total fragments reaching the destination [latex]=6[/latex] (from the split large fragments) [latex]+1[/latex] (the small fragment that passed through) [latex]=7[/latex].

Answer: 7

A packet with the destination IP address 145.36.109.70 arrives at a router whose routing table is shown. Which interface will the packet be forwarded to?
[latex]\begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Subnet Address} & \textbf{Subnet Mask (in CIDR notation)} & \textbf{Interface} \\ \hline 145.36.0.0 & /16 & E1 \\ \hline 145.36.128.0 & /17 & E2 \\ \hline 145.36.64.0 & /18 & E3 \\ \hline 145.36.255.0 & /24 & E4 \\ \hline \text{Default} & -- & E5 \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]

Routers use longest-prefix matching: find every subnet entry that contains the destination address, and among those, forward via the one with the most specific (longest) prefix.

Destination: [latex]145.36.109.70[/latex]. Check each entry:

Between the two matches (E1's [latex]/16[/latex] and E3's [latex]/18[/latex]), the [latex]/18[/latex] is more specific (longer prefix), so it wins.

Answer: E3

text: Consider the 3-way handshaking protocol for TCP connection establishment. Let the three packets exchanged during the connection establishment be denoted as P1, P2, and P3, in order. Which of the following option(s) is/are TRUE with respect to TCP header flags that are set in the packets?
solution:
TCP's 3-way handshake, packet by packet:

- P1 (client → server): the client initiates with SYN=1 (and ACK=0, since there's nothing to acknowledge yet).
- P2 (server → client): the server both acknowledges the client's SYN and sends its own SYN, so SYN=1, ACK=1 simultaneously (this combined SYN-ACK packet is the hallmark of TCP's handshake).
- P3 (client → server): the client only needs to acknowledge the server's SYN, so SYN=0, ACK=1 (not SYN=1,ACK=1 as one distractor suggests).

So the correct flags are P1: SYN=1, and P2: SYN=1 & ACK=1.

Answer: P2 (SYN=1, ACK=1), and P1 (SYN=1)

text: Which of the following statements about IPv4 fragmentation is/are TRUE?
solution:
